The Late Wars, 1982–2014

Seven battles from Goose Green in 1982 to Combat Outpost Keating in 2009: the paratroops at Darwin Hill in the Falklands, Eagle Troop at 73 Easting in the Gulf, the crash sites in Mogadishu, the Russian assault on the railway station in Grozny, the Marines and soldiers in Fallujah, and two American outposts in the mountains of north-east Afghanistan, at Wanat and Keating. Every rule is in the Rules; this book holds the armies' figures, the wound tables their battles roll on, and the battlefields.

The battlefields: Darwin Hill 1982, 73 Easting: Eagle Troop crests the rise 1991, Mogadishu: the crash sites 1993, Grozny: the railway station 1995, Fallujah: into the Jolan 2004, Wanat: the patrol base and the observation post 2008, Combat Outpost Keating 2009.

The period's fighting

This book covers the late wars of the twentieth century and the first of the twenty-first: the Falklands in 1982, the Gulf in 1991, Mogadishu in 1993, Grozny in 1994-95, and Iraq and Afghanistan from 2001 to 2014. Its battles run from Goose Green in May 1982 to Combat Outpost Keating in October 2009, and the game also has a table for Northern Ireland. Some of these wars were over in weeks. Others went on for years against an enemy who rarely stood to fight. In all of them a wounded soldier on the winning side had a better chance of living than in any war before.

Armies

The British and the Americans fought these wars with volunteers. The last British national serviceman was discharged to the reserve on 14 June 1963, the National Army Museum records, so the paratroopers and Royal Marines of 1982 were all regulars. The United States had ended the draft in 1973.

Not all of them served full time. The National Guard and the reserves were called up for Iraq and Afghanistan as never before. For much of 2005, the Guard Bureau said, the Army Guard provided half of the Army's combat forces on the ground in Iraq. In February 2006 General Peter Pace told the Senate that the Guard and reserves made up about 30% of the American forces in Iraq and Afghanistan. A Guard military police company from Kentucky fought the action at Salman Pak told below.

Argentina and Russia sent conscripts. The Argentine Army of 1982 had about 60,000 men, of whom 20,000 were regular officers and NCOs; most of the ranks were conscripts serving a single year. More than 10,000 soldiers went to the islands. Corbacho finds that some small Army units and the Navy's 5th Marine Battalion fought well, where officers, NCOs and conscripts held together. The Russian force that drove into Grozny on New Year's Eve 1994 was, in Oliker's words, made of conscripts and ad hoc units put together in haste. The army had held no divisional or regimental field exercise since 1992, and only five or six of the 151 hours of tactical training required before battle dealt with fighting in towns.

Against the regular armies stood insurgents and militias. The Chechens fought in small teams, Oliker writes: typically two men with RPG-7 or RPG-18 rocket launchers, two machine gunners and perhaps a sniper. Three such teams made a cell of about 25, and three cells a unit of about 75. They let the Russian columns in, then fought them at close range from cellars and the lower floors of buildings. The Somali militia in Mogadishu, the insurgents of Fallujah and the fighters who attacked Wanat and Keating fought in much the same way, from houses or hillsides, and wore no armour.

Arms

The British went to the Falklands with the 7.62 mm Self-Loading Rifle and the general-purpose machine gun, the GPMG; the Argentines carried the FN FAL, a rifle of the same family. In 1985 Britain accepted the 5.56 mm SA80. In the Gulf in 1991 it showed many faults: weak magazine springs, a magazine catch easily knocked, fragile firing pins. Heckler & Koch rebuilt about 200,000 of them from 2000, and the first rebuilt rifles went to Afghanistan in December 2001. The Americans kept the 5.56 mm M16 family. Against both, the Iraqis, Chechens, Somalis and Afghans carried the Kalashnikov.

American squads carried the SAW, the M249 Squad Automatic Weapon, adopted in February 1982 and issued to the Army from 1984 and the Marines from 1985. It fired the rifle's round from a belt at up to 850 rounds a minute. The British later gave the same gun, the Minimi, the machine-gun role in the section.

The RPG, the Soviet rocket-propelled grenade, was carried by every irregular army in this book. The Chechen teams had two each, and an RPG brought down the Black Hawk Super 61 in Mogadishu.

The Western armies had night-vision goggles and thermal sights, which see heat rather than light. In the sandstorm at 73 Easting in 1991, one American commander writes, the Iraqi tanks showed in his thermal sight only as hot spots, dug in with just their turrets showing. Nine M1A1 tanks and their Bradleys destroyed the position in about 23 minutes without loss. Armour was not safe in a town. In Grozny, Oliker writes, the Chechens halted Russian columns by knocking out the first and last vehicles, then fired down on the rest.

In Iraq and Afghanistan the weapon that wounded most was the improvised explosive device, the IED: a home-made bomb hidden by a road. Explosions caused 78% of American combat wounds from 2001 to 2005, Owens and colleagues found, more than in any large war before. The game's tables give the IED about 60% of all wounds.

Above it all flew precision weapons. In the Gulf only 8% of the tonnage dropped was guided, the US General Accounting Office found, though guided bombs were 84% of the cost. On the first night of the Afghan war, 7 October 2001, a Predator, a remotely piloted aircraft or drone, fired the first missile ever launched in combat from one; its crew sat in Virginia.

Battles

Some of these wars were short wars of manoeuvre. The Falklands war lasted 74 days, from the Argentine landing on 2 April 1982 to the surrender on 14 June. It cost 255 British and 649 Argentine lives. The Gulf war of 1991 was a 43-day air campaign followed by a ground war of 100 hours, in which American and British armour drove across open desert, as at 73 Easting.

Others were city fights. In Mogadishu on 3 October 1993 a raid by Task Force Ranger turned into a night-long fight for two crashed helicopters; 18 Americans died. In Grozny the Russian columns drove into the city on 31 December 1994 and lost most of their armour in its streets. At Fallujah in November 2004 American Marines and soldiers took the city house by house, with tanks firing into the buildings ahead of them.

Most of the fighting was at outposts and in counter-insurgency: patrols, checkpoints and convoys, the roadside bomb and the sniper, with a battle now and then when the enemy chose. Northern Ireland was the longest of these. The British Army's Operation Banner ran from 14 August 1969 to 31 July 2007, with about 21,000 troops there at its peak in the 1970s. The Ministry of Defence counts 1,441 service deaths; 722 of them were killed by paramilitaries. The army itself killed some 301 to 307 people, about half of them civilians. In eastern Afghanistan the Americans set small posts in the valleys, close to the villages. At Wanat in July 2008 and at Keating in October 2009 some 200 and 300 fighters attacked them from the hills at dawn.

Wounds and medicine

Soldiers wore more armour than ever before, and it stopped more. The Rangers in Mogadishu wore solid plates over the chest. No bullet or fragment went through those plates, Mabry and colleagues found, and chest wounds caused only 14% of their deaths from penetrating wounds, against 39% in Vietnam. But 36% of those deaths came from head wounds, all of them through places the helmet did not cover. From 2000 the Americans issued the Interceptor vest, with plates front and back rated to stop rifle bullets. Owens's figures for 2001-05 show the result. Wounds of the chest fell to 6%, against 13% in the Second World War and Vietnam; wounds of the head and neck rose to a larger share than in the Second World War, Korea or Vietnam; and 54% of wounds were to the limbs.

The tourniquet came back. It had long had a bad name, and in 2001 it was all but absent from American practice. Yet in Vietnam, Maughon found, 193 of 2,600 men killed in action had bled to death from a wound to a limb alone. In 1996 Butler, Hagmann and Butler published Tactical Combat Casualty Care, rules for care under fire written for special operations, built round the commonest causes of death that could be prevented. Its later guidelines called for the tourniquet to be used freely.

The tourniquet comes back

In the summer of 2004 the US Army Institute of Surgical Research in San Antonio tested nine tourniquets on 18 volunteers. Three worked best. The researchers chose the Combat Application Tourniquet, the CAT, because it was the quickest to learn: a strap tightened by a windlass and locked, which a man could put on his own arm with one hand. In January 2005 Central Command ordered its soldiers to carry one, and in March the Army Surgeon General had one issued to every soldier going to Iraq or Afghanistan. In Baghdad in 2006 John Kragh counted 232 casualties with tourniquets: 87% lived, and none of the five who needed one and did not get it. "There is no pre-hospital device deployed in this war that has saved more lives," said Colonel John Holcomb.

Speed mattered as much as the tourniquet. Forward surgical teams of about 20 people, Gawande wrote, could set up four beds and two operating tables within an hour, close behind the fighting. In 2009 the Pentagon ordered that a critically wounded man in Afghanistan reach a surgeon within the golden hour. Kotwal and colleagues found that the median helicopter flight fell from 90 minutes to 43, and the share of wounded who died fell from 13.7% to 7.6%; they put the lives saved at nearly 360.

From the combat hospital the chain ran by C-17 aircraft, with a doctor, nurse and respiratory therapist aboard for the worst cases, to Ramstein air base in Germany and the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center, a short drive away. Landstuhl treated nearly 66,000 patients from Iraq and Afghanistan from 2004 to 2012, about 14,000 of them with battle injuries. Gawande compared the 45 days a wounded man took to reach home from Vietnam with less than four.

The Red and Green Life Machine

On 22 May 1982 the British opened a field hospital at Ajax Bay, on San Carlos Water, in an old refrigeration plant built to freeze mutton. It stood beside an ammunition dump, and Brigadier Julian Thompson would not have a red cross painted on the roof. Two Argentine bombs lodged in it and did not go off; the surgeons worked on beneath them. Surgeon Commander Rick Jolly ran it, and Sea Kings brought the worst wounded in from the hills. The RAMC Association counts 580 British and Argentine patients; Thompson gave more than 650, and about 210 operations. Three died of their wounds, but none in its care. Its name, the Red and Green Life Machine, is said to come from the Paras' red berets and the Marines' green, or from its care for both armies.

The blast of the IED brought its own wounds. The Defense Department counted 383,938 first diagnoses of traumatic brain injury in American service members from 2000 to early 2018, 82% of them mild; the count includes injuries in training and at home. It counted 1,705 major amputations from the wars of 2001-17. Up to July 2011, Krueger and colleagues found, about 30% of amputees had lost more than one limb.

All this saved more of the wounded than in any war before. Gawande put the share who died at under 30% in the Second World War and about a quarter in Korea, Vietnam and the Gulf; in Iraq, he wrote, more than 90% of those hit were saved. Speed still depended on the fight: in Mogadishu medics cared for 39 casualties for more than 14 hours before they could be taken out.

Women

Women went further forward in these wars than ever before, though the rules still kept them out of the infantry and armour. No British servicewomen fought ashore in the Falklands. In the Gulf in 1991 the Americans sent between 33,000 and 41,000 women, by different counts. They flew helicopters, drove trucks, fired Patriot missiles and commanded companies. Thirteen died. Two were taken prisoner: Major Rhonda Cornum, a flight surgeon, and Melissa Rathbun-Nealy, an Army truck driver.

In Iraq the Americans needed women to search Iraqi women. Women were doing it in Ramadi in 2003-04, the first of the Lioness teams; in 2004-05 the Marines made the scheme formal, with volunteers who were mechanics, fuel handlers and clerks. On 23 June 2005 a suicide car bomb in Fallujah hit a truck carrying Lionesses back from the checkpoints. Six died, three of them women, and of 13 wounded, 11 were women. In Afghanistan from about 2009 the Marines formed Female Engagement Teams: two or three women attached to an infantry unit, living and patrolling with it, to talk with the women of the villages. They were barred from offensive patrols. The rule that kept women out of ground combat units was lifted on 24 January 2013.

Raven 42

On 20 March 2005 about 50 insurgents ambushed a supply convoy near Salman Pak, south of Baghdad. Its escort was Raven 42, a squad of the 617th Military Police Company, Kentucky Army National Guard, in three Humvees. Sergeant Leigh Ann Hester, a team leader, took her team into a flanking position. With her squad leader, Staff Sergeant Timothy Nein, she attacked a trench line with grenades and grenade-launcher rounds and cleared two trenches; she killed three men with her rifle. After about 30 minutes 27 insurgents were dead; none of the squad was killed. On 16 June 2005 Hester received the Silver Star, the first woman awarded it since the Second World War and the first ever for close combat. Nein and Specialist Jason Mike, the medic, received it too.

On the other side the record is thinner. Among Russian troops in Chechnya a story spread of the "White Tights", women snipers from the Baltic states hired by the Chechens. Regamey, who traced it, finds no evidence they existed; women taken in Chechnya were often labelled snipers whatever they had done. The Kurds were different. The PKK formed its first women's guerrilla units in 1995, and in Syria the Women's Protection Units, the YPJ, founded on 4 April 2013, fought in the defence of Kobanî in 2014, with American aircraft striking for them from October.

For the GM

Expect a fight in these wars to be short and lopsided in the open, and long and close in a town or a valley. A Western soldier has armour on his chest, a tourniquet in his pocket, a medic nearby and, after 2009 in Afghanistan, a helicopter within the hour: hits to the chest are rarer, and a man hit in the leg usually lives if the bleeding is stopped quickly. His face, neck, arms and legs are bare, and the roadside bomb takes legs. The Argentine and Russian conscript has a steel helmet and little else, and the Chechen, Somali or Afghan fighter has nothing; their wounded must be carried. In Mogadishu, Grozny and Fallujah, the wounded may wait hours or a night before anyone can reach them.

What is switched on

All three modern modules: Modern fire, Armour and mines and Air and night devices, with helicopters, landing by air and thermal sights. The wounded go out by helicopter where a landing zone and a helicopter are left, as the Rules' After the battle says. Wounds heal and fester as the Rules' Recovery says: it does not yet count the antibiotics, the tourniquets or the surgical teams of these wars.

Trouble at work

d10 Trouble
1 An IED or an ambush on the route.
2 The contract is cancelled, and the last month is never paid.
3 His name is on a militia death list.
4 A shooting incident: investigators and lawyers.
5 Kidnapped: the ransom is set at a year's pay.
6 A checkpoint shakedown: pay a bribe or lose the cargo.
7 The employer goes bust, or is banned from the country.
8 A mine strike or an unexploded bomb.
9 A co-worker is skimming or selling information, and he is blamed.
10 The local police arrest him, and his visa is in doubt.

What each skill is for

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Drive Drive under pressure: Drive off the road, at night without lights, or under fire. Ordinary — Through. Slowed or lost. Ditched or overturned.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Signals Get through: Raise another station, mend a line or a set, or send a message in code. Ordinary — Through. Not yet: try again next hour. The set or line is out until mended.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Battlefields

Each battlefield lays out on the field map under Battlefield. What follows is what the field and its phases hold, and, briefly, what happened there.

Darwin Hill, Goose Green, 28 May 1982

  • The armies: British and Argentines.
  • Fought for: the crest of Darwin Hill, attacked by the British.
  • The field: 140 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, breeze from the west, dusk.
  • Wounds: Falklands 1982 - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: Goose Green, 1982 (the Darwin isthmus), at Darwin Hill.

The campaign

Argentina occupied the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1982, and Britain sent a task force to retake them. On 21 May 3 Commando Brigade, under Brigadier Julian Thompson, landed at San Carlos on the west coast of East Falkland. Ships were lost to air attack in the days that followed; the Argentine Army's history of the battle says the British attacked the isthmus to reverse a run of losses that was wearing down support at home. On 26 May the 2nd Battalion, The Parachute Regiment (2 Para) was ordered south to the Darwin and Goose Green isthmus, where the Argentines held two settlements and an airstrip.

The battalion was commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Herbert "H" Jones. Its battle group, about 690 men on Wikipedia's count, had three 105 mm guns, a Milan platoon, Scout helicopters and the guns of HMS Arrow; Farrar-Hockley, who commanded A Company, put the battalion at about 450 men when it reached Camilla Creek House. The loss of the Atlantic Conveyor with most of the force's heavy-lift helicopters had left little artillery forward. On the eve of the attack the BBC World Service announced that 2 Para was about to attack Darwin and Goose Green.

Against them was Task Force Mercedes under Lieutenant Colonel Ítalo Piaggi: his 12th Infantry Regiment, less a company, C Company of the 25th Infantry Regiment under First Lieutenant Carlos Daniel Esteban, a section of the 8th Regiment, engineers, anti-aircraft guns and three 105 mm pack howitzers. The Argentine Army gives the task force 643 men on 27 May, with 202 Air Force men at Base Cóndor besides. About 100 islanders were held under guard in the Goose Green Social Club.

The places

  • Camilla Creek House: the farmhouse north of the isthmus where 2 Para gathered, and the forward base of the Scout helicopters.
  • Burntside House: the first objective, which A Company attacked in the dark; four islanders were found there unhurt.
  • Coronation Point: a headland on A Company's line of advance, found empty.
  • Darwin Hill: the ridge above Darwin settlement, with its gorse gully, where an Argentine company dug in with overhead cover and stopped A Company at first light.
  • Boca House: the ruined house at the west end of the ridge, where B Company was held, and which it took with Milan support.
  • Darwin: the small settlement on an inlet below Darwin Hill.
  • Goose Green: the larger settlement and airstrip to the south, where the islanders were held.
  • The schoolhouse: at Goose Green, near which Argentine aircraft were shot down in the late afternoon.
  • Mount Osborne: the height from which, Farrar-Hockley found afterwards, Argentine observers directed artillery onto the ridge.
  • San Carlos: the beachhead, from which the battalion came and to which its wounded went.

The leaders

  • H. Jones (British, lieutenant colonel, 2 Para): killed on Darwin Hill; awarded the Victoria Cross after his death.
  • Chris Keeble (British, major, second-in-command of 2 Para): took command after Jones's death, closed round Goose Green and arranged the surrender. He received the DSO.
  • Dair Farrar-Hockley (British, major, A Company): held in the gorse gully below Darwin Hill for more than three hours.
  • John Crosland (British, major, B Company): fought along the western side to Boca House.
  • Phil Neame (British, major, D Company): his company advanced between A and B Companies, and one of its platoons fought for the airfield in the afternoon.
  • Julian Thompson (British, brigadier, 3 Commando Brigade): ordered the attack on 25 May.
  • Ítalo Piaggi (Argentine, lieutenant colonel, Task Force Mercedes and 12th Infantry Regiment): commanded the garrison; wrote Ganso Verde (1986) in defence of his decisions.
  • Pedrozo (Argentine, air force, Base Cóndor): the senior Argentine officer at Goose Green, who surrendered the garrison to Keeble; naval-history.net gives his rank as group captain.
  • Carlos Daniel Esteban (Argentine, first lieutenant, C Company, 25th Infantry Regiment): his company held parts of the line; he was flown back to Goose Green during the battle.
  • Roberto Estévez (Argentine, lieutenant, platoon of C Company, 25th Infantry Regiment): led a counter-attack and was killed directing artillery fire; awarded Argentina's highest decoration for valour.

The battle

The British kept their signals on Zulu time (GMT), as the Ministry of Defence's files of 1982 show; the islands kept local time, four hours behind. The sources read here mostly print bare times. Wikipedia, after Fitz-Gibbon, marks its 13:13 for Darwin Hill as local, and the others read as local too, since they put the start in darkness and the first stand at first light. C Company and the engineers left at 22:00 on 27 May to clear the route. The attack began at about 03:35 on the 28th, after a delay in bringing in Arrow's fire. A Company took Burntside House, empty of Argentines, while B and D Companies went down the western side of the isthmus.

At first light the advance stopped. A Company was held under fire from the trenches on Darwin Hill and went to ground in the gorse gully; B Company was pinned on the bare slope short of Boca House. Wikipedia has A Company pinned from 09:00 to 10:00 and a third attempt beaten back at about 10:30. Farrar-Hockley puts the fight on the hill at something over three hours, against a company of 92 men with snipers and fixed-line machine guns. A sniper well back from the position, by Corporal David Abols's account, did much to hold the attack.

Jones came forward to the gully. He led a charge up a re-entrant, in which his adjutant Captain David Wood, A Company's second-in-command Captain Chris Dent and Corporal David Hardman were killed. He then went on alone at a trench and was shot from another he had passed. As he lay dying his men called for a helicopter. Two Scouts set out from Camilla Creek House; Pucarás caught them about five minutes after take-off, and shot down Lieutenant Richard Nunn's, killing him. Naval-history.net puts the loss at about 11:55.

A Company closed with the trenches using light anti-tank rockets and machine guns, and the Argentine company surrendered. A Company reported Darwin Hill taken at 13:13. B Company, with Milan, took Boca House at 13:47. Keeble pushed on towards Goose Green. In the afternoon D Company's 12 Platoon met fire near the airfield in which Lieutenant Jim Barry and two others were killed. Argentine aircraft attacked; a Blowpipe brought down an MB-339 at about 17:00. After last light Argentine helicopters landed a company of the 12th Regiment south of Goose Green, and J Company, 42 Commando, flew in to reinforce 2 Para.

In the night Keeble sent terms by two Argentine prisoners, and by CB radio through the Goose Green farm manager, with a deadline of 08:30 local. On 29 May Pedrozo agreed to surrender. Piaggi burned his regiment's colours, and the islanders were set free. Freedman's official history counts 961 prisoners, and says the count may not have been exact.

The battalion's dressing station dealt with nearly 80 British casualties on the 28th. The chief naval medical officer at San Carlos recorded 47 seriously wounded paratroopers who needed surgery under general anaesthetic, and the worst went on to the hospital ship Uganda. On Darwin Hill A Company's sergeant major, Colin Price, tended British and Argentine wounded together in the gully. The Argentine Army records its own helicopters landing at Goose Green under fire to take wounded out.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock. Wikipedia labels only two of its times; naval-history.net and the Argentine Army labels none. The Argentine Army's times (06:00 for Estévez's counter-attack, 08:30 for the withdrawal to the settlement, 12:30 for the final attack) do not match the British sequence, and its 2019 account dates the fighting to 29 May and the ceasefire to 11:00 on 30 May.
  • Argentine strength. Piaggi, as Fitz-Gibbon and Wikipedia give him, had 1,083 men in all. The Argentine Army gives 643 in the task force plus 202 of the Air Force; Wikipedia's table gives 903. Forces News says about 1,200.
  • British dead. Van der Bijl gives 18: 16 paratroopers, a Royal Marine pilot and a sapper. ParaData lists 15 of 2 Para killed on 28 May, naming Nunn and Corporal Mick Melia, RE, apart; naval-history.net and Forces News give 17.
  • British wounded. Wikipedia's infobox gives 64; Van der Bijl 33 paratroopers and a Royal Marine; naval-history.net 30 to 40. The dressing station dealt with nearly 80 casualties.
  • Argentine dead and wounded. Freedman gives 45, Boyce 55, Frontera 57; the Argentine Army names 12 dead of the 25th Regiment and 35 of the 12th. Wounded run from 86 to 145.
  • Who shot Jones. Snow and Snow point to Corporal Osvaldo Olmos; Bicheno to Corporal José Luis Ríos. Two conscripts of the 25th Regiment said that one of them shot him; Sergeant Barry Norman, beside him, thought it was a machine gun.
  • Jones's charge. His citation calls it an action of the utmost gallantry, and Margaret Thatcher called his death the turning point of the battle. Fitz-Gibbon argues that Jones did more to hinder than help, by not letting his company commanders fight their own battle.
  • Barry's death. Private John Graham says Barry went forward under a white flag and was fired on. Sub-Lieutenant Gómez-Centurión, the Argentine officer there, describes a British advance and makes no mention of a flag.
  • The islanders. MercoPress gives about 100 held in the Social Club for almost seven weeks; Wikipedia says over a hundred in the community hall.

Delta Romeo

Lieutenant Richard Nunn, Royal Marines, flew a Scout of 3 Commando Brigade Air Squadron with Sergeant Bill Belcher as his air gunner. From dawn on 28 May he and his flight commander, Captain Jeff Niblett, flew ammunition forward to 2 Para and brought wounded back, for three and a half hours. Then word came that the commanding officer was down. Both Scouts went forward again from Camilla Creek House. About five minutes out, two Pucarás attacked with cannon and rockets. Nunn dodged the first pass and was killed on the second. Belcher was thrown clear, badly wounded; Biggs says he lost a leg. Niblett evaded three more attacks and flew on until after dark. Both pilots received the Distinguished Flying Cross, Nunn's after his death.

How the field is drawn

Darwin Hill at dawn on 28 May 1982, at 10 m a hex: 140 x 110 hexes, about 1400 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: Darwin ridge across the middle with the Argentine trenches along its crest, the gorse gully below Darwin Hill on the right, a gorse hedge across the open slope, Darwin settlement by its inlet of Choiseul Sound in the lower right, Brenton Loch along the left. Light cover (scrub, key o): the gorse in the gully and the gorse hedge, seen and shot through at a cost. The ridge, the gully, the gorse, the shore and the settlement are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the fight at dawn, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Grey first light, a cold westerly, the peat wet underfoot.

73 Easting: Eagle Troop crests the rise, 26 February 1991

  • The armies: Coalition and Iraqis.
  • Fought for: the Iraqi position behind the rise at 73 Easting, attacked by the Coalition.
  • The field: 200 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 2,000 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Sandstorm, strong wind from the north-west.
  • Wounds: Gulf War 1991 (US) - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: 73 Easting, 1991 (the 2nd Armored Cavalry's last day), at the rise at 73 Easting.

The campaign

Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990. The coalition's air campaign began on 17 January 1991, and the ground offensive followed on 24 February, with H-hour at 03:00 Saudi time by the Center of Military History's reckoning. While the Marines and Arab forces pushed into Kuwait, the US VII Corps under Lieutenant General Frederick Franks swung west of the Wadi al Batin to strike the Republican Guard from the flank. Its lead was the 2nd Armored Cavalry Regiment under Colonel Leonard D. Holder, Jr. The regiment had screened the corps' front for weeks, and on the first day it breached the border defences.

The regiment's task was to find the Republican Guard ahead of the 1st Infantry Division and the armoured divisions behind it, without becoming decisively engaged. Each of its ground squadrons had three cavalry troops; each troop, Wikipedia says after the regimental accounts, had about 120 men, nine M1A1 Abrams tanks and twelve or thirteen M3 Bradley cavalry fighting vehicles. McMaster gives his own Eagle Troop, E Troop of the 2nd Squadron, as 130 soldiers, nine M1A1s, twelve Bradleys and two 120 mm mortars.

On the morning of 26 February the regiment's limit of advance was the 60 Easting, a north-south line on the military grid. At 05:22 a corps order moved it to 70 Easting and turned the attack on the Republican Guard. Rain in the night gave way to fog and then a sandstorm that grounded the air cavalry for half the day. Across the regiment's path, along the seam with the Iraqi 12th Armored Division, lay the Tawakalna Division of the Republican Guard. The IDA reconstruction names the unit in front of the 2nd Squadron as its 18th Brigade, guarding the division's flank.

The places

  • The Eastings: north-south grid lines 1 km apart used as phase lines; the regiment's limits of advance were the 60, then the 70 Easting.
  • The 67 Easting: Eagle Troop's own first limit, from which it set out east at 16:07.
  • The village: a fortified cluster of buildings, a training-area cantonment in the IDA paper, held with anti-aircraft guns and infantry; Eagle Troop's map did not show the road through it.
  • The first rise: the low ridge near the 70 Easting behind which an Iraqi tank company lay dug in on the reverse slope.
  • The 73 Easting ridge: about 3 km further east, where McMaster places the Iraqi reserve of 18 T-72s and the command post.
  • The 74 Easting: the line on which Eagle Troop halted at about 16:40.
  • The wadi at 73 Easting: a shallow valley to the north where Ghost Troop fought for about six hours into the night.
  • Phase line COLLINS: the line east of which the regiment advanced in the early afternoon, in the CMH account.

The leaders

  • H. R. McMaster (US, captain, Eagle Troop): commanded the troop from a tank in the centre of its wedge, and wrote two accounts of the fight (2016 and 2017).
  • Leonard D. "Don" Holder, Jr. (US, colonel, 2nd Armored Cavalry Regiment): commanded the regiment.
  • Frederick M. Franks, Jr. (US, lieutenant general, VII Corps): ordered the regiment to find the Guard but not to become decisively engaged.
  • Mike Kobbe (US, lieutenant colonel, 2nd Squadron): McMaster's squadron commander.
  • Douglas Macgregor (US, major, operations officer of the 2nd Squadron): rode with Eagle Troop; his tank struck a mine and was repaired on the move. He later wrote a book on the battle.
  • Craig Koch (US, staff sergeant, McMaster's gunner): destroyed the first tank seen once the troop crested the rise, then two more.
  • Tim Gauthier (US, lieutenant, Third Platoon): fired the first TOW into the village; later said the main fight ended in 23 minutes.
  • Joe Sartiano (US, captain, Ghost Troop): commanded the troop to Eagle's north.
  • Major Mohammed (Iraqi, commander of the defence in front of Eagle Troop): McMaster names him as a graduate of the Infantry Officer Advanced Course at Fort Benning; no other source read gives his full name or unit.

The battle

Times are those of the American accounts, which give no clock for this action. The CMH gives the start of the ground war in Saudi time (GMT+3), and the accounts read as that clock. By McMaster's account, Eagle Troop moved off at 16:07 in a modified column. The scout platoons led in Bradleys, the mortars followed, and the nine tanks came behind in a wedge. At 16:07 Staff Sergeant John McReynolds' Bradley drove onto an Iraqi observation bunker and two soldiers came out to surrender. His wingman, Sergeant Maurice Harris, then came under 23 mm and machine-gun fire from the village. Gauthier fired a TOW into its centre, Koch marked it with a tank round, and all nine tanks put high explosive into it. The IDA paper has contact with dismounted Iraqis near the cantonment at 16:15.

A TOW from Staff Sergeant David Lawrence's Bradley hit what turned out to be a T-72. The tanks then crested the rise. Stars and Stripes, after the veterans, gives the time as 16:19; Wikipedia gives about 16:20. Koch reported eight T-72s in prepared positions at close range, killed the first, and then two more. The troop fought through the trenches and bunkers behind them.

While the troop was still clearing the western positions, Lieutenant John Gifford, the executive officer, reported that it had reached the 70 Easting limit. McMaster ordered the attack on, judging that a halt would give the Iraqis time to recover. The tanks crested the next rise as the reserve was starting to move, and destroyed it at close range; McMaster has this from about 16:40. Stars and Stripes says the troop halted just short of the 74 Easting at 16:40. Gauthier put the main fight at 23 minutes. The IDA paper puts the main fight at about 90 minutes, with fighting going on for six hours.

After dark the Iraqis sent a company of T-72s and BMPs at the ridge, which was destroyed at long range. To the north Ghost Troop beat off attacks in the wadi until about 21:00, its fire support team calling down 720 howitzer and rocket rounds. There a BMP-1's 73 mm round hit the turret of a Bradley whose TOW was out of action and whose cannon had jammed, and killed its gunner, Sergeant Nels A. Moller. The 1st Infantry Division passed through the regiment's lines just after 22:00.

Eagle Troop had no casualties. Its medics treated and evacuated Iraqi wounded, and guards held the prisoners, several hundred by McMaster's count, through the night; some had expected to be shot. Wikipedia gives the regiment's losses in the whole battle as 6 killed and 19 wounded, and records an I Troop Bradley hit by a TOW from K Troop, which wounded all three crewmen.

Where the accounts disagree

  • Eagle Troop's tally. McMaster, in both his accounts, gives about 50 T-72s, 25 armoured personnel carriers and 40 lorries. Wikipedia gives two figures: 28 tanks, 16 carriers and 30 lorries in 23 minutes, and elsewhere eight tanks in the first position and 18 at the 74 Easting. Stars and Stripes adds 13 more destroyed by a scout patrol.
  • The Iraqi position. McMaster gives about 40 tanks and 16 BMPs, hundreds of infantry and an 18-tank reserve. The IDA reconstruction's database for the whole 2nd Squadron fight holds 55 T-72s, 33 BMP-1s, 147 dismounted men with 19 RPG-7s, and assumed 21 empty berms. Its actual Iraqi losses are 57 tanks, 28 BMPs, 11 MT-LBs and 45 lorries.
  • The Iraqi units. The IDA paper names the 18th Armored Brigade of the Tawakalna; Wikipedia calls it the 18th Mechanized Brigade. McMaster adds elements of the 10th Armored Division. The CMH puts the fight at the seam between the Tawakalna and the 12th Armored Division.
  • How long it lasted. Gauthier and McMaster: 23 minutes for the main fight. IDA: about 90 minutes, with fighting for six hours. The CMH has the regiment find the tanks "just after 1600" and the battle end at 17:15, yet speaks of four hours of fighting.
  • The regiment's total. The CMH gives at least 29 tanks and 24 carriers destroyed and about 1,300 prisoners. Wikipedia, after the regimental history, gives 159 tanks, 260 other vehicles and about 2,000 prisoners.
  • Why it went so one-sidedly. The IDA's Janus replication (1992) ran the battle again with changes. With clear weather the exchange came out about even; with thermal sights on both sides it turned about two to one in Iraq's favour. Its authors conclude that American thermal sights were a major cause of the result. They used a 400 m sight limit for the sandstorm.
  • Iraqi accounts. No Iraqi account of this fight in English was found. McMaster's picture of the Iraqi plan is his own.

Tell them we can't stop

Eagle Troop had broken the first Iraqi position and was still clearing its trenches when Lieutenant John Gifford, the troop's executive officer, came on the radio. The troop had reached the 70 Easting, its limit of advance. McMaster judged that if he halted, the Iraqis behind the next ridge would have time to recover and fight. He told Gifford to tell the squadron that the troop could not stop, and added an apology. The nine tanks went on and crested the next rise as the Iraqi reserve was moving out. McMaster later wrote that the decision came from a command climate that expected junior leaders to act on mission orders.

How the field is drawn

The rise at 73 Easting on the afternoon of 26 February 1991, at 10 m a hex: 200 x 120 hexes, about 2 km east to west (from about 72.2 to 74.2 Easting on the military grid) and 1.2 km north to south, north at the top: flat, hard desert, a low rise running north to south across the left middle with the Iraqi trenches and dug-in tanks on its reverse (east) slope, hidden by it (dead ground), and the high ground about 74 Easting on the right. The rise, the trenches and the high ground are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the moment before Eagle Troop crested the rise, just out of the dug-in tanks' sight, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A sandstorm: sight cut to 400 m, thermal sights included (a design choice; in the event the M1A1s' thermal sights saw further than the Iraqis' could), a strong wind. No aircraft fly in it. No minefields are drawn: the accounts we used name none on this ground.

Mogadishu: the crash sites, 3 October 1993

  • The armies: United States and Somali National Alliance.
  • Fought for: Super 61's crash site, attacked by the Somali National Alliance.
  • The field: 110 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,100 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the south-west, night.
  • Wounds: Somalia 1993 - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: Mogadishu, 1993 (the airport to the stadium), at Crash site 1 (Super 61).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 783 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

In May 1993 the United Nations force UNOSOM II took over in Somalia from the American-led UNITAF. On 5 June militia of Mohamed Farrah Aideed's Somali National Alliance (SNA) ambushed Pakistani soldiers of UNOSOM II in Mogadishu, killing 24. The next day the Security Council passed Resolution 837, which the US Army's Center of Military History (CMH) calls a more aggressive stance towards Aideed. The UN's special representative, Admiral Jonathan Howe, put a price of $25,000 on information leading to Aideed's arrest, and through the summer American and UN troops raided SNA targets in the city.

In late August Task Force Ranger arrived, under Major General William F. Garrison of Joint Special Operations Command. It answered not to the UN but directly to General Joseph Hoar of Central Command. Wikipedia gives its parts as B Company, 3rd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment (Captain Michael D. Steele); C Squadron, 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta (Lieutenant Colonel Gary L. Harrell); 16 helicopters of the 1st Battalion, 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment; and Navy SEALs and Air Force pararescuemen and combat controllers of the 24th Special Tactics Squadron. The UN's quick reaction force was the 2nd Battalion, 14th Infantry, 10th Mountain Division, under Lieutenant Colonel William C. David. That September the Secretary of Defense, Les Aspin, turned down a request from Major General Thomas Montgomery, the American commander, for tanks and armoured vehicles.

On the afternoon of Sunday 3 October word came that two of Aideed's lieutenants, Omar Salad Elmi and Abdi Hassan Awale, would meet in a building near the Olympic Hotel, close to the Bakara Market in the heart of Aideed's Habr Gidr clan. Delta would land at the building from MH-6 Little Birds, Rangers would fast-rope from Black Hawks to block the four corners, and a convoy of Humvees and trucks under Lieutenant Colonel Danny McKnight would carry the prisoners out. The raid was planned to take no more than 30 minutes.

The places

  • The target building: a house near the Olympic Hotel, a few blocks north of the Bakara Market.
  • The Bakara Market: the city's largest market, in the clan's own district; Captain Haad says its people joined the fight.
  • Crash site 1: where Super 61 came down, about three blocks from the target by the CMH's account; the Rangers and Delta held the houses round it all night.
  • Crash site 2: where Super 64 came down, less than a mile to the south; overrun about an hour after the crash.
  • The airport: Task Force Ranger's compound, about four minutes' flight from the target.
  • The K-4 traffic circle: where the 10th Mountain's first company was pinned down in the evening.
  • The New Port: where the relief column of Pakistani, Malaysian and American troops formed up.
  • National Street: the road the relief column came in by; two Malaysian carriers that turned off it were ambushed.
  • The Pakistani stadium: the UN base where the force came out at dawn and the wounded were treated.

The leaders

  • William F. Garrison (United States, Task Force Ranger): commanded from the airport; later wrote to President Clinton accepting full responsibility.
  • Thomas Montgomery (United States, US forces and deputy UN force commander): asked for armour in September and was refused.
  • Danny McKnight (United States, 3rd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment): led the ground convoy.
  • Michael D. Steele (United States, B Company, 3rd Battalion, 75th Rangers): led the Rangers on the ground.
  • William C. David (United States, 2nd Battalion, 14th Infantry): led the 10th Mountain troops of the relief column.
  • Michael Durant (United States, chief warrant officer, pilot of Super 64): the one man from his crash site to live; held prisoner until 14 October.
  • Gary I. Gordon and Randall D. Shughart (United States, master sergeant and sergeant first class, Delta snipers): defended crash site 2 and were killed; awarded the Medal of Honor.
  • Mohamed Farrah Aideed (SNA, leader): the man the task force had come to catch; died of wounds in August 1995.
  • Sharif Hassan Giumale (SNA, colonel): named by Wikipedia as the SNA's tactical commander in the battle.
  • Captain Haad (SNA, sector commander): led about 30 militiamen that day and later told his story to PBS Frontline.
  • Abdul Latif Ahmad (Malaysia, commander, Malaysian Battalion): his memoir gives the Malaysian account of the relief, led by Major Abdul Aziz's Alpha Company.

The battle

The American accounts give local time (East Africa Time, GMT+3), and so do the times here. At 13:50 the code word went out. The helicopters lifted off at about 15:30, the convoy three minutes behind, and at 15:42 the assault force was at the target. Private First Class Todd Blackburn fell from his rope and was badly hurt; three Humvees took him back, and Sergeant Dominick Pilla was shot dead in one of them, the first American killed. The assault force took 24 prisoners. By Haad's account the militia had been warned from the airfield that helicopters were on their way to a serious attack, and fired at them as they flew low; men took cover under sheets held up by women and boys.

At about 16:20 Super 61, flown by Chief Warrant Officer Clifton Wolcott, was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade and came down about three blocks away. Both pilots were killed. A Little Bird landed beside the wreck and flew out two wounded men. The combat search and rescue team, 15 men under Captain Bill Coultrup, fast-roped in from Super 68, which was hit by a grenade as they went down but got back to the airport. The assault and blocking forces went to the crash on foot. The convoy could not find the site, lost two 5-ton trucks, and went back to the airfield with its prisoners and wounded.

At about 16:40 Super 64, Durant's aircraft, was hit in the tail rotor and came down less than a mile to the south. No ground force could reach it soon. Gordon and Shughart asked three times to be put down there, and were landed from Super 62, which was then hit by a grenade and crash-landed. Their Medal of Honor citations say they pulled the four badly hurt crew from the wreck, held a perimeter until their ammunition ran out, and were killed; Gordon gave the pilot a rifle with its last rounds. The citations say they saved Durant's life. The site was overrun at about 17:40, and Durant was taken prisoner.

The force round crash site 1 held a block of houses through the night, with Little Birds firing for them in pairs. The pararescuemen set up a casualty collection point by the tail of the wreck and lined it with the Kevlar floor panels torn from the aircraft. Technical Sergeant Timothy Wilkinson freed the surviving crewmen from the wreck. At about 17:30 he crossed an open crossroads three times to treat about a dozen men, and Master Sergeant Scott Fales, shot through the leg, worked beside him. Corporal James Smith, a Ranger, was hit in the thigh; the bullet cut his femoral artery. The men round him could not get him out, and he bled to death, his father said, over about three hours. At 19:08 Super 66 brought in water, ammunition and medical supplies and was badly damaged.

A company of the 2nd Battalion, 14th Infantry went out in the evening, was pinned down near K-4 and went back. The relief column formed at the New Port, with Pakistani tanks in the lead and Malaysian armoured carriers behind, more than 60 vehicles by the CMH's count, with Cobra gunships overhead. Two Malaysian carriers with the 2nd Platoon of A Company, 2nd Battalion, 14th Infantry turned south off National Street and were ambushed; their men took cover and were reached about four hours later. Lance Corporal Mat Aznan Awang of the 19th Battalion, Royal Malay Regiment, driving one of them, was killed when a rocket came through the window. At 01:55 on 4 October the Malaysian carriers and the 10th Mountain troops reached crash site 1. Another part of the column reached crash site 2 and found no trace of the crew or the snipers.

The men at crash site 1 worked through the night under fire to free Wolcott's body from the wreck. The wounded were loaded into the carriers. At 05:42 the move out began, and with no room in the vehicles many men ran and walked behind them, the "Mogadishu Mile". The main force reached the Pakistani stadium at about 06:30, where the medical staff gave the wounded emergency treatment. Wilkinson's carrier, which stopped for about 90 minutes to pick up another casualty, came in at about 08:00. On 7 October President Clinton set 31 March 1994 as the date by which all American forces would leave Somalia.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The American losses. The CMH gives Task Force Ranger 16 killed and 57 wounded, and the 2nd Battalion, 14th Infantry 2 killed and 22 wounded: 18 killed and 79 wounded. The Special Operations Command's own history of 1994 gives the task force 16 killed and 83 wounded. PBS Frontline and the National Museum of the US Air Force give 18 killed and 84 wounded; Wikipedia gives 84 in its summary and 73 in its text.
  • The Malaysian and Pakistani losses. The CMH gives 2 Malaysians killed and 7 wounded, and 2 Pakistanis wounded. Wikipedia gives 1 Malaysian killed and 7 wounded; its article on Mat Aznan Awang, 1 killed and 9 wounded. Abdul Latif Ahmad, as the Borneo Post reports him, gives 1 killed and 6 hurt.
  • The Somali losses. The CMH puts them at 500 to 1,500. The Special Operations Command history gives the Red Cross estimate of about 200 dead and 700 wounded, and Radio Mogadishu's figure of 364 killed and 754 wounded. Wikipedia gives the SNA's figure as 315 dead, 133 of them its own fighters, and 812 wounded; Haad gave the same 133 for the militia. Ambassador Robert Oakley's own estimate was 1,500 to 2,000 killed and wounded.
  • Civilians. No source read separates the Somali civilian dead from the fighters: by the SNA's figures in Wikipedia about 180 of its 315 dead were not fighters, and Haad called the civilian deaths "almost uncountable".
  • The Pakistani tanks. The CMH has the tanks lead the column. Abdul Latif says they would not go on because they had no night sights, and the Malaysians moved to the front.
  • When the relief left. Wikipedia's timeline has the column move out at 23:23 and its main article at about 23:00; Abdul Latif, as reported, says the Malaysian operation began at about 20:30.
  • The size of the column. The CMH says more than 60 vehicles; Wikipedia about 100. Abdul Latif gives 113 Malaysians, of whom Alpha Company had 5 officers and 42 other ranks.
  • Where Super 61 fell. The CMH says about three blocks from the target; Wikipedia's main article about 300 yards east, and its timeline about four blocks north.
  • When Super 64 fell. Wikipedia gives about 16:40; Haad remembered about an hour after the first, around 17:00.
  • How Gordon and Shughart died. Gordon's citation has Shughart killed first. Wikipedia says Bowden's account, through Sergeant Paul Howe, who heard Shughart call for help on the radio, and Durant's own book differ on the order and on which weapon Durant was given.
  • The second lieutenant's name. Wikipedia gives him as Abdi Hassan Awale in one place and Mohamed Hassan Awale in another.
  • The armour. Aspin refused Montgomery's request for tanks, and said afterwards that he would have decided otherwise had he known what he knew later. Stars and Stripes reports that the Senate review co-written by Senator John Warner in 1995 found that tanks "may well have saved U.S. lives".

The crossroads

Technical Sergeant Timothy Wilkinson was a pararescueman with the rescue team that fast-roped down to Super 61. He went into the wreck and freed the two surviving crewmen, though he was hit in the face and arm by fragments. The team tore out the Kevlar floor panels to wall in the wounded at the tail. At about 17:30 word came that men across an open crossroads were hurt. Wilkinson ran across three times under fire, treating about a dozen men, one with a wound to the hip and groin that he dressed with pressure bandages, pneumatic trousers, morphine and a drip. At dawn he rode out with the wounded in a Malaysian carrier. He received the Air Force Cross, the first to an enlisted airman since 1975.

How the field is drawn

The streets round the target and the two crash sites in Mogadishu on the evening of 3 October 1993, at 10 m a hex: 110 x 110 hexes, about 1100 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the target building left of the middle, the Olympic Hotel down the street from it on Shalalawi Street, the Bakara Market to the south-west, the first crash site to the north-east and the second to the south. The street plan, the houses, the walled yards and the taller buildings are drawn by hand, not traced from any map or photograph: narrow sand streets (open ground), one-storey stone houses behind walls (buildings), the hotel and a few blocks of several storeys (tall buildings), the market's stalls and sheds. The deployment is nightfall, in our own words, with round numbers for play. It is dark (the moon rose late that night); the Little Birds fly at night. The two downed Black Hawks are on the map (downed helicopters). There are no vehicle rules: the relief column can be brought on as infantry from the south with Add a unit.

Grozny: the railway station, 31 December 1994

  • The armies: Russians and Chechens.
  • Fought for: the railway station, attacked by the Chechens.
  • The field: 140 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, calm or light air, dusk.
  • Wounds: Chechnya - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: Grozny, 1995 (the New Year's assault), at Grozny railway station.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 1531 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

When the Soviet Union broke up, Chechnya, under its president Dzhokhar Dudayev, declared itself independent of Russia. Through 1994 Moscow backed Chechen opponents of Dudayev, and their attacks on Grozny in August, October and November failed; in November their tank columns were surrounded in the city and destroyed by men with rocket launchers. In December 1994 Russian troops moved into Chechnya. Wikipedia gives the defence minister, Pavel Grachev, as having boasted that he could take Grozny in two hours with one airborne regiment.

The force that gathered round the city was, by Oliker's account for RAND, built of conscripts and units thrown together in haste, few of whom had trained together; the army had held no divisional or regimental field exercise since 1992, and its maps were too few and of the wrong scale. Oliker describes a plan for armoured columns to drive on the city centre from the north, east and west. Wikipedia names the groups and their commanders: North under Major General Konstantin Pulikovsky, North-East under Lieutenant General Lev Rokhlin, West under General Ivan Babichev and East under Major General Nikolai Staskov, with Lieutenant General Anatoly Kvashnin over them. The ring round the city was never closed, and the south stayed open.

The Chechens had had three or four months to prepare, and they knew their city. Their chief of staff, Aslan Maskhadov, a former Soviet officer, commanded the defence; Shamil Basayev and Ruslan Gelayev led groups of fighters. Estimates of their strength run, in Oliker's words, from about 1,000 to ten times that. Before the assault the Chechen headquarters moved out to Shali.

On 31 December 1994 about 6,000 Russian soldiers, Thomas says out of some 38,000 round the city, drove into Grozny. Among them were the 131st Separate Motor Rifle Brigade from Maykop, under Colonel Ivan Savin, about 1,000 men by Thomas's count, and the 81st Guards Motor Rifle Regiment under Colonel Yaroslavtsev.

The places

  • The railway station: in the city centre; the 131st Brigade's 1st Battalion went into it on the afternoon of 31 December.
  • The streets round the station: where the brigade's vehicles parked in columns, the reserve on a side street.
  • The railway line: the way the brigade's remnants tried to break out after midnight.
  • The presidential palace: Dudayev's seat in the city centre, the 81st Regiment's objective; it fell on 19 January 1995.
  • The city centre: blocks of flats of five and nine storeys and older houses, where the Chechen teams waited in basements and upper floors.
  • The southern edge of the city: never closed, so the Chechens could bring men and supplies in through the battle.
  • Shali: the town to the south-east where the Chechen headquarters went before the assault.

The leaders

  • Pavel Grachev (Russian, defence minister): drew up the plan of three stages for the invasion.
  • Anatoly Kvashnin (Russian, lieutenant general): commanded the assault force.
  • Konstantin Pulikovsky (Russian, major general, Group North): Wikipedia places both the 131st Brigade and the 81st Regiment under him.
  • Lev Rokhlin (Russian, lieutenant general, Group North-East): reached the centre from the north but could not reach the trapped units.
  • Ivan Savin (Russian, colonel, 131st Separate Motor Rifle Brigade): held the station until 1 or 2 January; killed trying to bring out his wounded.
  • Yaroslavtsev (Russian, colonel, 81st Guards Motor Rifle Regiment): led the column towards the palace; Wikipedia names Burlakov as his chief of staff.
  • Dzhokhar Dudayev (Chechen, president): led the breakaway republic.
  • Aslan Maskhadov (Chechen, chief of staff): planned the defence; Wikipedia gives him the plan of letting the tanks into the centre and striking at nightfall.
  • Shamil Basayev and Ruslan Gelayev (Chechen, field commanders): led groups of fighters in the city.

The battle

The times here are those the sources give; none says which clock it keeps, but Grozny kept Moscow time (GMT+3), and the sunset at about 16:30 fits. Thomas says the columns entered at noon and met no resistance at first. The vehicles drove straight to the centre. The 131st Brigade's 1st Battalion, the first unit to reach it, got down and took up positions inside the railway station, while other vehicles stood parked on a side street as a reserve. The Russian accounts summarised on Wikipedia have Russian battalions at the station by about 13:00 and close to the palace by about 15:00, almost without a fight, and the columns standing in the streets with no defence organised, no posts and no patrols out.

The Chechen fighters came in from other parts of the city and closed round the station. Oliker describes how they fought: squads of a few men with rocket launchers, machine guns and perhaps a sniper, three squads to a cell of about 25 and three cells to a unit of about 75. Teams of six or seven waited in the lower floors of buildings, keeping 50 to 250 m from the Russian columns. They knocked out the first and last vehicles in a street, and Thomas notes that the tanks' guns could neither depress far enough to reach the basements nor rise high enough to reach the roofs. Oliker says it took three to six hits to destroy a tank. Grau, for the Foreign Military Studies Office, puts the armoured columns' losses at 105 of 120 tanks and carriers.

The 81st Regiment's column, on its way to the palace, was ambushed and lost most of its armour. In the Russian accounts given on Wikipedia, the fighting round the station began at about 19:00 and went on all night, and the troops fell back into the station building, which was poor ground to defend. At about midnight the remnants of the brigade, with two tanks, tried to break out along the railway; from about 01:00 on 1 January there was no more contact with them, and they were reported surrounded and destroyed. Savin, by Thomas's account, waited for help until 2 January, and none came. Wikipedia gives his death as 2 January.

Savin tried to get his wounded out. An armoured carrier took 40 of them; it was ambushed, and 13 men lived to be taken prisoner. Grau and Thomas describe how the Russians moved their wounded in the weeks that followed: in BTR-80 carriers used as ambulances, because the Chechens fired on soft-skinned ones, to aid posts and hospitals dug in or in basements, since those were shelled too. Snipers often kept the wounded from being moved until dark. They write that most of the wounds came from mortars, that burns were more common than in other wars, and that most of the killed were hit in the head or chest by snipers. One participant, Oliker says, put up to 60 per cent of the Russian casualties down to their own side's fire.

By 3 January the brigade had lost most of its men and vehicles. The Russians fell back, brought up artillery and took the city block by block. They took the palace on 19 January. The Chechens left Grozny in February and March.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The 131st Brigade's losses. Thomas says that by 3 January it had lost nearly 800 men, 20 of its 26 tanks and 102 of its 120 armoured vehicles. Wikipedia's main article gives about 789 killed and 75 captured. Its article on the palace assault cites Lukin for 189 killed, captured or missing, with the same 20 tanks and 102 vehicles and all six Tunguska anti-aircraft vehicles. Its article on the brigade, after Krasnaya Zvezda (2006), gives 85 killed and 72 missing, 157 in all, and 22 T-72 tanks, 45 BMP-2s and 37 other vehicles lost.
  • The Russian losses in the New Year assault. Carlotta Gall, in the New York Times as Wikipedia cites her, put them at least 1,500 and perhaps 2,000 over sixty hours. Oliker says only that they fell by the hundreds.
  • The armour. Grau gives 105 of 120 tanks and carriers lost in the first columns. Wikipedia gives General Galkin's count of 225 armoured vehicles past repair, 62 of them tanks, in the first six weeks; Maskhadov claimed about 400.
  • The Chechen strength. Oliker gives estimates from about 1,000 to about 10,000; Grau says about 12,000 fought in Grozny over the whole battle; the Russian account on Wikipedia has up to 3,500 men, 50 guns and tanks and 300 grenade launchers gathered against the centre.
  • The Chechen losses. Wikipedia gives Russian official figures of 6,690 Chechen fighters killed between December 1994 and April 1995, and Western estimates in the low thousands for the whole battle. No source read gives a figure for the night at the station.
  • Civilians. Estimates of the civilians killed in Grozny vary widely: Anatol Lieven put them at about 5,000, Sergei Kovalev, President Yeltsin's human rights adviser, at about 27,000 in the five weeks of fighting, many of them ethnic Russians, and the World Peace Foundation at 25,000 to 30,000 by mid-February 1995, as Wikipedia gives them.
  • When the fighting began. Thomas has the column cut off soon after it arrived; the Russian account on Wikipedia has the fighting begin at about 19:00. Our game starts it at dusk, about 16:30.
  • The end at the station. The Russian account on Wikipedia has the breakout along the railway at about midnight and contact lost at 01:00 on 1 January. Thomas has Savin waiting for help until 2 January, and Wikipedia gives his death as 2 January. Our game has the survivors break out at about 18:00 on 1 January.
  • Who went to the station. Oliker gives the station to the force from the west. Wikipedia puts the 131st Brigade in Group North. One passage on Wikipedia has a battalion of the 81st Regiment at the station by 13:00; most accounts send the 81st to the palace.
  • The total Russian losses. Wikipedia's infobox gives the official figure for the whole battle as 1,834 killed, 4,670 wounded and 96 captured; its text gives 1,376 killed and 408 missing; Western estimates run to more than 5,000 killed.

The last carrier

Colonel Ivan Savin commanded the 131st Brigade, and he was with it in the station when the Chechens closed round it on the night of 31 December. By Thomas's account he waited for reinforcements until 2 January, but none got through. Savin had 40 of his wounded loaded into an armoured carrier to try to get them out. The carrier was ambushed. Thirteen men lived, and were taken prisoner. Savin was killed that day, with almost the whole of the brigade's command. Krasnaya Zvezda, the army's newspaper, counted 24 of the brigade's officers dead.

How the field is drawn

The railway station in Grozny at dusk on 31 December 1994, at 10 m a hex: 140 x 110 hexes, about 1400 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the station building in the middle with its square to the north, the platforms, tracks and freight yard to the south, older houses round the station, and apartment blocks of five and nine storeys beyond, with streets between. The square, station, yards, tracks and blocks are drawn by hand to that pattern, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is the fight for the square at dusk, in our own words, with round numbers for play. The apartment blocks are tall buildings (tall buildings), the houses buildings; vehicles keep to the square, the streets and the tracks. Winter dusk, the dark coming on: the phases bring a dark night at about 17:05 (sunset about 16:30, the moon a day from new, worked out for the place and day). The objective is the Chechens': the night was their attack on the station.

Fallujah: into the Jolan, 9 November 2004

  • The armies: Coalition and Insurgents.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 140 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, breeze from the north-west.
  • Wounds: Iraq & Afghanistan 2001-05 - combat wounds.
  • On the travel map: Fallujah, 2004 (Operation Phantom Fury), at the Jolan.

The campaign

On 31 March 2004 insurgents ambushed four armed security contractors of Blackwater USA there. A crowd burned the bodies and hung two from the Old Bridge over the river. Lieutenant General Ricardo Sanchez ordered an attack, although Lieutenant General James Conway and Major General James Mattis of the Marines urged restraint. On 5 April Colonel John Toolan's Regimental Combat Team 1 (RCT-1) closed a cordon round the city, and on the 6th the 2nd Battalion, 1st Marines attacked into the Jolan, the old north-western quarter. The Marines halted on 9 April and pulled out in early May. They left the city to the Fallujah Brigade, an Iraqi force under former Ba'athist officers, which broke up and gave its weapons to the insurgents.

Over the summer Fallujah became the base of Abu Musab al-Zarqawi and of insurgent groups under Abdullah al-Janabi and Omar Hadid. The Marines reckoned there were 3,000 to 4,500 fighters by late October, with more than 300 prepared positions, many of them mined or booby-trapped. Planning for a second attack began in September. Lieutenant General John Sattler's I Marine Expeditionary Force gathered nine American battalions and six Iraqi ones, about 12,000 men. The Marines asked for Army armour, and the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry came from Taji with 14 tanks and 30 Bradleys. Leaflets and broadcasts told the people to leave, and most did.

On the night of 7 November Iraqi commandos took the hospital and Marines the bridges west of the city. The next night two regimental combat teams attacked south across the railway: RCT-1 in the west through the Jolan, RCT-7 to the east. The Americans called the operation Phantom Fury; after Prime Minister Ayad Allawi was briefed in late October it was renamed al-Fajr, "New Dawn".

The places

  • The Jolan: the old north-western quarter by the river, of narrow, irregular lanes and walled houses.
  • The railway and the train station: the northern edge of the city and RCT-1's start line; the breach was cut in the embankment west of the station.
  • The apartment complex: the blocks north of the railway, taken by 3/5 on the 8th, from which Colonel Shupp watched the assault.
  • The Jolan cemetery and the Ma'ahidy Mosque: 3/5's first objectives on the night of 8 November.
  • Jolan Park: the one open space in the quarter, with a Ferris wheel that could be seen from afar, and the 2-7 Cavalry's objective.
  • Phase Line Henry: the north-south road down which the Army armour drove.
  • Phase Line Fran and the Martyrs' Cemetery: Highway 10 across the middle of the city, and the cemetery on it.
  • The hospital and the bridges: on the peninsula west of the river, taken on the night of 7 November.

The leaders

  • John F. Sattler (Coalition, lieutenant general, I Marine Expeditionary Force): took over from Conway on 12 September 2004.
  • Richard F. Natonski (Coalition, major general, 1st Marine Division): commanded the assault.
  • Michael A. Shupp (Coalition, colonel, RCT-1): the Marine main effort, in the west of the city.
  • Patrick J. Malay (Coalition, lieutenant colonel, 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines): attacked into the Jolan along the river.
  • Willard A. Buhl (Coalition, lieutenant colonel, 3rd Battalion, 1st Marines): followed the Army armour to clear the houses.
  • James E. Rainey (Coalition, lieutenant colonel, Task Force 2-7 Cavalry): argued for a wider front than the first plan gave him.
  • Peter C. Glass (Coalition, captain, C Company, 3rd Battalion, 8th Cavalry): led the night attack to Phase Line Fran.
  • Robert J. Bodisch Jr. (Coalition, captain, C Company, 2nd Tank Battalion): found the breach sites and led the Marine tanks.
  • Abdullah al-Janabi (Insurgents): led one of the groups that ruled the city after the spring.
  • Omar Hadid (Insurgents): led another; Wikipedia gives him as killed in November 2004.

The battle

Times are as the Marine history gives them, presumably local Iraq time (GMT+3); no source read names the clock. At about 14:00 on 8 November four F/A-18Ds dropped eight GBU-31 bombs to cut the railway west of the overpass. Company L of 3/1, with a company of the Iraqi National Guard, took the train station and held it by 20:34. The line charges failed to clear the lanes, so engineers cut the rails with TNT and bulldozers pushed them aside. At 19:26 3/5 went in through the cut. Company I cleared the Jolan cemetery and took the Ma'ahidy Mosque; Company L pushed along the river towards the palm groves.

At 00:14 on 9 November C Company, 3rd Battalion, 8th Cavalry crossed the breach and led Task Force 2-7 down Phase Line Henry; the rest followed at 01:30. The chemical lights marking the lanes did not show in the Bradleys' thermal sights. Before sunrise A Company, 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry drove from the station and took Jolan Park, its tanks and Bradleys shooting into the buildings. Company K of 3/1 came in at 04:00 and Company I by 06:00, with Company L behind in reserve.

The Marines cleared house by house behind the armour. Captain Timothy Jent of Company K kept two platoons forward, one with the vehicles and one lighter platoon to guard a flank or carry out the wounded. The insurgents aimed their rockets at the tanks' tracks, sights and bore evacuators. At about 08:30 one disabled Bodisch's tank. Company L of 3/1 lost two Marines in a house where insurgents waited for them, and met mortars firing from underground near Phase Line Cathy. Company I reached Phase Line Donna at about 12:30, passed through A Company of 2-7, and held its objective for nearly five hours under rifle and rocket fire. In the afternoon Bodisch came back in a fresh tank to help Marines of Company I hit by snipers in a building. In 3/5's sector the Marines fought at 50 to 100 m for about four hours that morning.

At about 18:00 3/5 halted for the night, and 3/1 stopped level with Phase Line Cathy at Jolan Park. There snipers killed a Marine and an Iraqi soldier. At about 23:00 Rainey sent Glass's company down Henry and onto Fran, to the Martyrs' Cemetery. A mosque beside it fired on them. Glass's call for artillery or air was refused, and Apaches of the 4th Aviation Brigade silenced the fire. The task force was on Highway 10 ahead of the plan. On the 10th 3/5 took what one Marine's citation calls the last strongpoint in the Jolan, and by 13 November most of the heavy fighting in the city was over, though the clearing went on into December.

The sources read say little of the battalion aid stations; the companies carried their own wounded back, Jent's lighter platoon among them, and some of RCT-7's went out through the Army's breach. Alpha and Bravo Surgical Companies were at Al Asad and Camp Fallujah, and a surgical shock trauma platoon at Camp Taqaddum. In the first six days of the offensive that platoon alone took 157 patients, 29 of them Iraqis, and operated 73 times; at the peak four surgeons did 46 operations in 12 hours. Most of the wounds were blast and gunshot, 75 to 80 per cent in the arms and legs. Patients went on by CH-46 helicopter, with nurses aboard, to the next level of care, the combat surgical hospitals; the blood came forward by helicopter from the hospital in Baghdad, and many of the wounded were kept under anaesthetic all the way to Landstuhl in Germany.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The April operation. Estes, for the Marines, and Wikipedia call it Vigilant Resolve; Matthews, for the Army, calls it Valiant Resolve. Wikipedia gives 27 Americans killed in its text and "39+" in its table.
  • The dead in April. McWilliams gives about 220 Iraqi civilians killed in the first two weeks. Wikipedia, after Iraq Body Count, gives about 800 Iraqi dead, 572 to 616 of them civilians. Ahmed Mansour of Al Jazeera, who was in the city, reported heavy civilian losses.
  • Who was left in the city. McWilliams says the Marines believed fewer than 500 civilians remained by late October. Wikipedia gives an American estimate of 30,000 to 90,000 left of about 300,000, and a Guardian correspondent's 30,000 to 50,000.
  • The insurgents. Matthews puts them at about 2,000 in April; McWilliams at 3,000 to 4,500 in October, with about 1,000 more nearby; Wikipedia's table at 3,700 to 4,000. A senior US official in September put Zarqawi's forces at about 5,000, mostly not Iraqis.
  • The losses. Wikipedia gives 54 Americans killed and 425 wounded from 7 to 16 November, and 95 killed and 560 wounded by 23 December, with 8 Iraqi soldiers killed. It gives the insurgent dead as about 1,200 by the Defense Department's count, 1,500 by Asia Times, and more than 2,000 by some estimates, with about 1,500 captured.
  • The civilian dead. The Red Cross was reported on 17 November 2004 as fearing about 800 civilians dead; Iraq Body Count records 581 to 670 from bodies recovered in nine of the city's 27 neighbourhoods; and Mike Marqusee in the Guardian (November 2005), as Wikipedia gives him, quoted Iraqi aid groups and medical workers estimating 4,000 to 6,000 dead, mostly civilians.
  • Who led the Jolan attack. The game has 3/1 coming in behind the Army armour and its own Marine tanks, as McWilliams has it. He also has 3/5 attacking along the river from 19:26 on the 8th, some hours before the armour crossed; it was 3/1 that followed the 2-7 Cavalry.

The last strongpoint

On 10 November Private First Class Christopher Adlesperger of Company K, 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines went into a house in the Jolan with his squad. A machine gun inside killed the point man and wounded two others. By his Navy Cross citation, Adlesperger, himself hit by grenade fragments, fought his way up the stairs and onto the roof and got the wounded out. He set up firing positions there that kept the insurgents pinned in the house or drove them into the fire of the Marines next door. He then took the point for the last assault and was the first man back into the courtyard. The citation calls the house the last strongpoint in the Jolan. He was promoted lance corporal in a lull in the fighting, and was killed in action the next month, before the award was made.
