Wanat: the patrol base and the observation post, 13 July 2008

  • The armies: United States and Insurgents.
  • Fought for: Observation Post Topside, attacked by the Insurgents.
  • The field: 90 by 70 hexes of 10 m, about 900 by 610 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, dusk.
  • Wounds: Iraq & Afghanistan 2001-05 - combat wounds.
  • On the travel map: Wanat, 2008 (the Waygal valley), at Wanat (Vehicle Patrol Base Kahler).

The campaign

American troops came to the valleys of Kunar and Nuristan, on the Pakistan border, in strength in April 2006. In Operation Mountain Lion the 3rd Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division (Task Force Spartan) moved in, and its 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry built outposts in the Pech, Korengal and Waygal valleys. In the Waygal, Lieutenant Colonel Christopher Cavoli put Combat Outpost Ranch House near Aranas and Combat Outpost Bella near the hamlet of that name, each held by half a platoon; the Combat Studies Institute (CSI) says Bella was picked partly because a medical clinic run by a charity stood there. In July 2006 troops of the 3rd Squadron, 71st Cavalry also landed at Kamdesh, to the north, where the base later named Keating grew up. In September and October 2006 American engineers, with about 50 local labourers, built a new bridge at Wanat. Ambushes and roadside bombs killed six Americans in the Waygal that year, among them Captain Douglas Sloan.

In May 2007 the 2nd Battalion (Airborne), 503rd Infantry of the 173rd Airborne Brigade, Task Force Rock, took over, with Chosen (C) Company in the Waygal. Bella could be reached only by helicopter, 16 km from Forward Operating Base Blessing on the Pech. In January 2008 Sergeant First Class Matthew Kahler of Chosen Company was shot dead by an Afghan soldier; Wikipedia says the death was ruled an accident. A new district centre was finished at Wanat in June 2008. Through June and early July Bella was harassed and there were reports of fighters massing. On 4 July an American helicopter attacked vehicles near Bella that it said were firing on it; 17 people were killed, and Wikipedia gives reports that they were civilians, among them the staff of a clinic.

Chosen Company was near the end of its tour, and Bella was to be given up. In Operation Rock Move, on the nights of 8 and 9 July, 1st Platoon was flown out of Bella, and 2nd Platoon of Chosen Company drove up from Blessing to build a new base beside the district centre at Wanat, about 8 km away. It was named Vehicle Patrol Base Kahler. With the paratroopers came engineers, Marine trainers and a platoon of the Afghan National Army. The engineers' Bobcat loader broke down for a day, so the barriers were about 4 feet high, not the 7 intended, and much of the digging was done by hand. The Afghan contractor's heavy equipment was due on 13 July.

The places

  • Vehicle Patrol Base Kahler: the new base, an open field about the size of a football pitch beside the road and the district centre.
  • Observation Post Topside: a post on the terraces east of the base, held by nine men; it had a northern and a southern fighting position.
  • The draw: a brush-filled gully running past the north side of Topside, about 10 yards from the post.
  • The bazaar and the hotel: north of the base; the first machine-gun burst came from a two-storey building on that side.
  • The mosque and the village: Wanat's houses on the terraces to the west, from which the fighters also fired.
  • The traffic-control point: at the base, where a casualty collection point was set up.
  • Forward Operating Base Blessing: on the Pech near Nangalam, about 8 km away; its two 155 mm guns fired for Wanat, and the quick reaction force drove from there.
  • Combat Outpost Bella: up the valley, given up in Operation Rock Move.
  • Camp Wright: where the wounded were flown, and where the helicopters were refuelled and rearmed.

The leaders

  • Jonathan Brostrom (United States, 1st Lieutenant, 2nd Platoon): the platoon leader; killed taking ammunition up to Topside.
  • David Dzwik (United States, Staff Sergeant): 2nd Platoon's platoon sergeant.
  • Matthew Myer (United States, Captain, Chosen Company): commanded from the command post in the middle of the base.
  • Ryan Pitts (United States, Sergeant, forward observer): directed the guns from Topside and held the post when he was the last man left there; Medal of Honor in 2014.
  • Jeffrey Scantlin (United States, Specialist): a combat lifesaver who took over as medic when the medic was hit; Silver Star.
  • William Ostlund (United States, Lieutenant Colonel, 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry): commanded Task Force Rock.
  • Charles Preysler (United States, Colonel, 173rd Airborne Brigade): reprimanded in 2010 with Ostlund and Myer; the reprimands were withdrawn.
  • Dost Mohammad, Maulavi Uthman and Sadiq Munibullah (Insurgents): named by Wikipedia as the attackers' leaders; nothing more about their parts is given in the sources read.

The battle

Times here are local, Afghanistan time (GMT+4:30, with no summer time); the sources do not say which clock they kept, but they read as local time. The platoon stood to at 04:00 on 13 July. Through the TOW's thermal sight men saw figures on the high ground to the west, and Pitts and Sergeant Matthew Gobble began a request for artillery. At about 04:20 a machine gun opened from a two-storey building to the north, and Military Times says about 20 RPGs followed. The fire came from the bazaar, the hotel, the mosque, the village and the hills, and Wikipedia says about 100 more fighters came at Topside from the farmland to the east. The mortar pit was hit and the 120 mm mortar knocked out, its ammunition set off, and an RPG destroyed the TOW.

At Topside, fighters in the draw hit the post with rifles, RPGs and grenades, and the Army's narrative says all nine men there were wounded; Specialists Matthew Phillips and Gunnar Zwilling were killed. Pitts, hit in both legs and his left arm, threw grenades, fired the M240 and later an M203, and reported by radio to Myer while he called the guns from Blessing onto targets planned round the post. At about 04:45 Brostrom and Specialist Jason Hovater ran up from the base. They were killed, as were Corporals Jason Bogar and Pruitt Rainey. Pitts then found himself alone at the northern position. A second party, Staff Sergeant Sean Samaroo, Sergeant Israel Garcia and Specialists Michael Denton and Jacob Sones, reached the post and was caught by an explosion; Garcia died. Three times teams ran from the base through the fire to bring up ammunition and bring down the wounded.

The Apaches and an armed Predator arrived, by Wikipedia's account, about 30 minutes in. A danger-close gun run let a third party take the post. The 1st Platoon of Chosen Company drove up from Blessing as a quick reaction force and cleared fighters from the village and the hills. Blessing's guns fired 96 rounds. Later B-1B, A-10 and F-15E aircraft came on, and Wikipedia says the fighters drew off about four hours after the attack began. The base was given up a few days later.

The wounded were gathered at two casualty collection points: one at Topside's southern position, the other at the traffic-control point in the base. The platoon medic, Private First Class William Hewitt, was shot in the arm after about half an hour, and Scantlin, trained as a combat lifesaver, took over his work. RAND notes that most of the American losses came at Topside or on the runs to it to bring up ammunition and carry down the wounded. At about 06:15 a medical evacuation helicopter landed under fire and took out Pitts, Samaroo, Sones and Denton. The wounded were flown to Camp Wright.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The Americans' strength. The CSI foreword gives 49 Americans and 24 Afghan soldiers; RAND gives 48 soldiers, 3 Marines and 24 Afghans; the army.mil graphic gives 48 Americans. Ricks, writing of the CSI draft, speaks of 42 soldiers and 3 Marines.
  • The insurgents' strength. The Army's narrative says about 200. Wikipedia says the Americans first thought 100 to 200, and that an Afghan defence official spoke of 400 to 500. Military Times says more than 100.
  • How long it lasted. Wikipedia and the CSI speak of about four hours; RAND of nearly nine, until enough air strikes could be brought in; Military Times of about 90 minutes.
  • The air support. Wikipedia has the Apaches and an armed Predator overhead about 30 minutes in. RAND says high winds grounded the unmanned aircraft. A commenter on Small Wars Journal (Cole) says the Apaches and medical evacuation helicopters came within the hour after a 29-minute flight. The game puts the Apaches at about 05:20, the medical evacuation helicopter at 05:52 to 06:05 and the quick reaction force at 06:01; the Army's narrative puts the evacuation of Pitts at about 06:15.
  • The danger-close strike. The army.mil battle page puts it about 10 m from the Americans; the narrative on DVIDS says about 30 m.
  • The losses. All give 9 Americans killed. The infobox and RAND give 27 wounded and 4 Afghans wounded; the Army's 2010 release says "27 casualties". The Americans claimed 21 to 65 fighters killed and 20 to 45 wounded, but Wikipedia says only two bodies were found. A Taliban claim reported in the Pak Tribune spoke of 20 Americans killed.
  • The province. Wanat is in the Waygal district of Nuristan; the army.mil Medal of Honor page puts it in Kunar.
  • Who was to blame. The first investigation (August 2008) found the fighters had help from the local police and a district leader. Ricks says the CSI draft (2009) found failures by the battalion and brigade commanders; Wikipedia says the final study (2010) laid the weight on the uncertainty of war, junior officers' mistakes and a poor grasp of local politics and intelligence. After a Central Command review under Lieutenant General Richard Natonski, General Charles Campbell began adverse action against Preysler, Ostlund and Myer in March 2010; in June he found them neither negligent nor derelict and withdrew it.

The last man at Topside

Sergeant Ryan Pitts was the forward observer at Topside. The first volley wounded him in both legs and his left arm and killed two men beside him. He threw grenades, fired the machine gun, and kept talking on the radio to his company commander, bringing the guns at Blessing down on the ground round the post. When the men who had come up to help were killed or had gone down wounded, he found himself alone at the northern position. He fought on with an M203 grenade launcher for more than an hour, badly wounded, until the next party and the Apaches came. He was flown out at about 06:15. He received the Medal of Honor on 21 July 2014. He said it belonged to everybody who was there that day.

How the field is drawn

The patrol base and the observation post at Wanat at dawn on 13 July 2008, at 10 m a hex: 90 x 70 hexes, about 900 m east to west and 600 m north to south, north at the top: the base (an open field about 100 m by 300 m) right of the middle, Observation Post Topside on the ridge east of it, the brush-filled draw past the post's north side, the bazaar and hotel to the north, the village and its mosque on the terraces to the west, the Waygal river and the high ground beyond. Light cover (scrub, key o): the brush in the draw, seen and shot through at a cost. The fields, terraces, houses and slopes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is about 04:20, in our own words, with round numbers for play. First light (dusk or dawn). The base's barriers were chest-high at best and in places only loose wire: the paratroopers are dug in (gone to ground), the fighters firing from cover. The 120 mm mortar and the TOW were hit in the first minutes; the Apaches came about half an hour in, the jets later.

Combat Outpost Keating, 3 October 2009

  • The armies: Coalition and Insurgents.
  • Fought for: the outpost, attacked by the Insurgents.
  • The field: 120 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,200 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, dusk.
  • Wounds: Iraq & Afghanistan 2001-05 - combat wounds.
  • On the travel map: COP Keating, 2009 (the Kamdesh valley), at Combat Outpost Keating.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 671 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

The base at Kamdesh in Nuristan was set up in July 2006, when troops of the 3rd Squadron, 71st Cavalry landed there, and it was named Camp Keating that December after Lieutenant Benjamin Keating, killed when his vehicle went off the road in November. It sat at the bottom of a deep valley, overlooked by high ground. Convoys up the Landay-Sin road were ambushed again and again, and by 2009, Wikipedia says, it was being supplied by air only on moonless nights. The nearest attack helicopters were at Jalalabad, about 30 minutes' flight away. A year before, in July 2008, nine Americans had been killed at Wanat in the same region, and the Jamestown Foundation's Hassan Abbas set the two attacks side by side.

In 2009 the outpost was held by B Troop, 3rd Squadron, 61st Cavalry, of the 4th Brigade Combat Team, 4th Infantry Division, with a platoon on Observation Post Fritsche on the ridge to the south. Afghan National Army soldiers held the east side, advised by Latvian mentors, and Afghan police and hired Afghan guards stood at the gate and in checkpoints. Plans to close the outpost went back to December 2008. The Army's investigation says it was to close in July or August 2009, but the helicopters needed to carry the stores out were sent to fighting at Barg-e Matal, to the north. General Stanley McChrystal, commanding in Afghanistan, meant to draw troops in from the remote valleys to the towns. In late September, by the Defense Media Network's account, the troop was told it would close on 10 October.

The investigation counts about 47 attacks on the outpost in B Troop's five months there, about three times the rate its predecessors had faced. Because earlier warnings of massing fighters had come to nothing, it says, the intelligence staffs had grown used to them, and with closing near, little was done to improve the defences. The attackers were local Taliban and men of Hezb-e-Islami Gulbuddin; the Long War Journal names Mullah Abdul Rahman Mostaghni, the Taliban military commander for Kamdesh and Barg-e Matal, and Dost Mohammed. Nuristan's governor told the Associated Press that fighters had come in after Pakistani troops drove them out of Swat.

The places

  • Combat Outpost Keating: a cluster of buildings on a flat by the river, ringed with wire and overlooked by high ground on every side.
  • Observation Post Fritsche: the platoon post on the high ground about 1,500 m south, attacked at the same time; its 120 mm mortars covered the river.
  • Urmul: the village across the Landay-Sin, where an interpreter reported 50 to 100 fighters gathering at dawn.
  • Kamdesh: the district's main village on the mountainside above; its mosque, about half a mile up the slope, was a main source of fire until it was bombed.
  • The entry control point: the main gate, held by hired Afghan guards, where the fighters broke in.
  • LRAS 1 and LRAS 2: fighting positions named after their long-range sights; LRAS 1 was on the north side, and at LRAS 2 a Humvee crew was cut off for hours.
  • The aid station: with the command post; once the fighters were inside, the gate was the only way left to reach it.
  • Forward Operating Base Bostick: in Kunar, where the wounded were flown after dark, and from there to Bagram.

The leaders

  • Stoney Portis (Coalition, Captain, B Troop, 3-61 Cavalry): the troop commander; later admonished or reprimanded with three other officers.
  • Andrew Bundermann (Coalition, 1st Lieutenant, B Troop): named by Wikipedia among B Troop's commanders that day; his Silver Star was raised to the Distinguished Service Cross.
  • Clinton Romesha (Coalition, Staff Sergeant, section leader): led the counter-attacks that took back the gate and the ammunition point; Medal of Honor, 2013.
  • Ty Carter (Coalition, Specialist, scout): fought from the cut-off Humvee at LRAS 2 and brought in a wounded man; Medal of Honor, 2013.
  • Jonathan Hill (Coalition, Sergeant First Class): platoon sergeant; gave covering fire to open the way to the aid station.
  • Justin Gallegos (Coalition, Staff Sergeant): led the men in the Humvee at LRAS 2 and was killed breaking contact; his Silver Star was raised to the Distinguished Service Cross.
  • Chris Cordova (Coalition, Captain): gave trauma care at the aid station.
  • Jānis Laķis (Coalition, First Sergeant, Latvian mentor team): with Corporal Mārtiņš Dāboliņš, tried to keep the Afghan soldiers from running.
  • Abdul Rahman Mostaghni (Insurgents, Taliban commander for Kamdesh and Barg-e Matal): reported killed by an air strike on 9 October; the Taliban denied it.
  • Dost Mohammed (Insurgents): named by Wikipedia as the Taliban's shadow commander in Nuristan.

The battle

Times here are local, Afghanistan time (GMT+4:30, with no summer time); the sources do not say which clock they kept, but they read as local time. At about 03:00 on 3 October, Wikipedia says, more than 150 fighters told the people of Kamdesh to leave. At 05:53 an interpreter told Private First Class Jordan Wong that 50 to 100 fighters were in Urmul. At 05:58 or 05:59 fire came in from every side: heavy machine guns, B10 recoilless rifles, RPGs, mortars and rifles. The mortar pit was put out of action at once, and the first American was hit within two minutes. Fritsche was attacked at the same time and could give little help.

Romesha went to LRAS 1 and then took a machine gun towards LRAS 2. An RPG hit a generator beside him and he was wounded. At LRAS 2, at about 06:30, Staff Sergeant Justin Gallegos decided to break contact; Carter stayed with Sergeant Bradley Larson to cover the others, and Gallegos was killed as they moved. About 48 minutes in, the fighters broke into the outpost in three places: at the main gate, where the guards were overwhelmed; on the east side, where the Afghan soldiers gave way; and, Wikipedia says, by the latrines. They set the buildings alight. Within the first hour the Americans and Latvians had drawn into a tight inner perimeter.

From there they pushed out again. Romesha killed three fighters inside the wire, led five men to the ammunition supply point, and with Hill's men took back the shura building and the gate. He called in air strikes that the citations credit with more than 30 fighters killed. Apaches, A-10s, a B-1 and F-15Es struck the slopes and the mosque; two F-15Es stayed overhead for nearly eight hours and brought in 19 other aircraft. Fighters held parts of the outpost as late as 17:10. Men of the 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry were flown to Fritsche at about 14:00, walked down, met an ambush at about 18:00, and reached the outpost at about 19:00, where they found Sergeant Joshua Hardt dead.

The wounded could not be flown out while the fight went on. At about 07:30 Carter reached Specialist Stephan Mace, wounded by RPG fragments, stopped the bleeding with a tourniquet and carried him to the Humvee. Mace reached the aid station only at about noon, after Romesha and Hill had opened a way. Captain Cordova kept him alive with fluids and six transfusions of blood given by men of the troop, Cordova himself among them. Heavy fire kept the medical evacuation helicopter from landing until dark. Mace was flown to Bostick and on to Bagram, where he died. The investigation says B Troop destroyed the outpost on 6 October before leaving, and Wikipedia that a B-1 bombed the remaining stores that day; Abbas says Fritsche and COP Lowell were given up with it, four days after the attack.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The attackers. The investigation and both citations give about 300. The American Legion magazine gives nearly 350; the Long War Journal more than 350.
  • The defenders. Wikipedia's infobox gives 53 Americans, 42 Afghan soldiers and 2 Latvians; the Army's 2013 article 50 Americans and 2 Latvians, with 19 Americans at Fritsche; the American Legion fewer than 60 cavalrymen; Abbas about 50 Americans and 90 Afghan police.
  • The losses. All give 8 Americans killed. The investigation gives 22 wounded, all but three back on duty; Wikipedia 27, the number of Purple Hearts awarded; Abbas 24. Wikipedia gives 8 Afghan soldiers and 2 guards wounded; the Associated Press and the Long War Journal up to 7 Afghans killed. The AP says the Taliban took 15 Afghan police, among them the police chief. The investigation gives at least 150 fighters killed; Wikipedia and the American Legion 150 to 200.
  • The helicopters. The Long War Journal, after an American officer, has them overhead about 45 minutes in; Wikipedia has them by the afternoon.
  • How long it lasted. The Army's 2013 article says about 10 hours, the American Legion about 12, the Romesha page 13. The game runs until about 17:10, when the last fighters were cleared from the outpost.
  • Where they broke in. The Defense Media Network has the west side breached first; Wikipedia names the gate, the east side and the latrines.
  • The Taliban's account. The Taliban, in Al-Sumud, called Keating one of the biggest American bases, which Abbas thinks overstated. Zabiullah Mujahid claimed the attack and said the Americans had destroyed the bases and would not come back.
  • The blame. The investigation found the attack was made easier by inadequate measures taken by the chain of command; four officers were admonished or reprimanded. The Long War Journal notes that a Taliban video showed much left behind, though the report said the base was destroyed.

A hundred metres to the aid station

Specialist Ty Carter was cut off in a Humvee at LRAS 2 with Sergeant Bradley Larson. At about 07:30 he saw Specialist Stephan Mace lying wounded about 30 m away, ran out to him, stopped the bleeding and put on a tourniquet, and carried him back to the truck. For hours they could not move him. When Romesha and Hill's men opened a way, Carter and Larson carried Mace about 100 m under fire to the aid station. He reached it at about noon, some five hours after he was hit. There Captain Chris Cordova gave him six transfusions of blood from the men of the troop. The helicopter could not land until dark. Mace died after he was flown to Bagram. Carter received the Medal of Honor in 2013.

How the field is drawn

Combat Outpost Keating at dawn on 3 October 2009, at 10 m a hex: 120 x 110 hexes, about 1200 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the outpost on its flat in the middle, ringed with wire, the Landay-Sin down the left with the bridge to Urmul, the Kushtoz coming in from the east below the outpost, and steep slopes of rock, scrub and deodar rising on every side. Light cover (scrub, key o): the scrub on the lower slopes among the rock; the deodar above is woods. The flat, the buildings, the river, the stream, the village and the slopes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is the attack at dawn, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Observation Post Fritsche, on the ridge to the south-east, is off this field.
